readings.context: Recap: Matthew realized that Anne was never dressed like the other girls, failed comically to buy a dress himself, and asked Mrs. Lynde to make one with puffed sleeves for Christmas. Marilla does not know yet. Aunt Josephine is Diana’s rich great-aunt in Charlottetown, the island’s capital, whom Anne won over after the girls jumped onto her in the spare-room bed. A waist is a bodice; shirring is gathered fabric; an ulster is a long overcoat; kid slippers are made of soft leather. To be encored is to be called back to perform again. Queen’s is the academy in Charlottetown that trains teachers.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXV, from Christmas Eve and the finished dress to the end of the chapter; opens “Marilla knew all the following fortnight that Matthew had something on his mind, but what…”; closes “…and on,” said Matthew. “Things like that are all the better for lots of thinking over.””.

questions.prompt: Marilla calls the dress “sheer extravagance.” How does she behave when Anne opens it, and what does the narrator show that Marilla does not say?
facilitatorNotes: She pretends to be busy with the teapot but watches “with a rather interested air,” and she passes on the matching ribbon. Her words disapprove; her eyes and actions show interest and care. Readers can find other places where Marilla hides her feelings.
evidence: who feigned to be contemptuously filling the teapot, but nevertheless watched the scene out of the corner of her eye with a rather interested air
I must say, Anne, I don’t think you needed the dress

questions.prompt: Anne says she “must live up to those sleeves.” How does the dress help her at the concert? Is that a sensible reason for courage?
facilitatorNotes: Faced with “a million eyes,” she thinks of the sleeves and takes heart; she also admits that practising in the garret got her through. Clothes can change how confident we feel, but practice did the work. Readers may find her reasoning silly, honest or both.
evidence: Then I thought of my lovely puffed sleeves and took courage. I knew that I must live up to those sleeves, Diana.
It’s providential that I practised those recitations so often up in the garret

questions.prompt: Diana tells Anne that Gilbert picked up the rose from her hair. How does Anne answer, and do you believe her?
facilitatorNotes: She says it is “nothing to me what that person does” and that she never wastes a thought on him, without even using his name. A reader may suspect she protests too much; the story has not yet shown what she really feels.
evidence: I saw Gil pick it up and put it in his breast-pocket.
It’s nothing to me what that person does,” said Anne loftily.

questions.prompt: Matthew and Marilla are both proud of Anne. What is the difference between them, and what are they beginning to plan?
facilitatorNotes: Matthew told Anne he was proud; Marilla admits it only to Matthew and will not tell her. Matthew thinks she will need more than the Avonlea school, and Marilla is already thinking of Queen’s. The scene shows Marilla’s reserve, Matthew’s openness, and how much both now care about Anne’s future.
evidence: Anyhow, I was proud of Anne to-night, although I’m not going to tell her so.
Well now, I was proud of her and I did tell her so ’fore she went up-stairs

readings.title: Elaine on the pond (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xxviii, part 1 of 2)
readings.challenge: Compare a scene from a poem with what happens when the girls act it out.
readings.focus: Anne plays Tennyson’s Elaine on the pond, and romance turns into danger.
readings.context: In L. M. Montgomery’s Anne of Green Gables (1908), the orphan Anne Shirley lives with Marilla and Matthew Cuthbert at Green Gables in Avonlea, Prince Edward Island. Anne, now thirteen, loves anything romantic and still holds a grudge against Gilbert Blythe, who once called her “Carrots” in school. Not long before, a bottle of hair dye turned her red hair green, and it had to be cut short. The girls act a scene from Alfred Tennyson’s “Lancelot and Elaine,” one of his Idylls of the King, in which Elaine, the “lily maid,” dies for love of the knight Lancelot and her body is carried on a barge, draped in black samite (a rich silk), to King Arthur’s court at Camelot. A flat or dory is a small flat-bottomed boat; Orchard Slope is the Barrys’ farm; Idlewild was the girls’ playhouse in a grove.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXVIII, “An Unfortunate Lily Maid,” from the choosing of Elaine to Anne’s plight in the leaking flat; opens ““Of course you must be Elaine, Anne,” said Diana. “I could never have the courage to…”; closes “…to the lips, but she did not lose her self-possession. There was one chance—just one.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Anne think she should not play Elaine, and why does she agree to anyway?
facilitatorNotes: Elaine is a golden-haired “lily maid,” and Anne thinks a red-haired one “ridiculous”; her “artistic sense” wants the part to fit. But the others are afraid to lie still in the boat, and Diana’s remark that her hair is darker now pleases her. She cares about how the scene looks as much as about the starring role.
evidence: Now, a red-haired person cannot be a lily maid.
her artistic sense demanded fitness for it and this, she felt, her limitations made impossible

questions.prompt: The class had “analyzed and parsed” Tennyson’s poem until little meaning was left. What does the game on the pond do for the girls that the lessons did not?
facilitatorNotes: Acting it out makes Elaine, Lancelot and Guinevere “very real people.” The girls find stand-ins for the poem’s splendour: a black shawl for samite, a piano scarf for cloth of gold, an iris for a lily. The narrator gently mocks lessons that pull a poem to pieces; readers may compare their own experience of studying poems.
evidence: They had analyzed and parsed it and torn it to pieces in general until it was a wonder there was any meaning at all left in it for them
Cloth of gold for coverlet there was none, but an old piano scarf of yellow Japanese crêpe was an excellent substitute.

questions.prompt: Ruby asks whether it is “really right to act like this.” How does Anne answer, and what does the exchange show about how each girl plays?
facilitatorNotes: Ruby is frightened that Anne looks “really dead” and repeats Mrs. Lynde’s view that play-acting is wicked. Anne objects only that mentioning Mrs. Lynde “spoils the effect”: she wants the illusion kept whole. Ruby’s fear also hints that the game is closer to danger than the girls know.
evidence: Oh, she does look really dead,” whispered Ruby Gillis nervously
It spoils the effect because this is hundreds of years before Mrs. Lynde was born.

questions.prompt: Where does romance turn into danger? How does the writing change at that point?
facilitatorNotes: “Then something happened not at all romantic.” Elaine has to scramble up holding her “pall of blackest samite” while water pours through a crack, and the poem’s grand words now sound comic beside it. Short questions and answers (“Where were the oars?”) speed up the alarm, though Anne keeps her self-possession.
evidence: Then something happened not at all romantic. The flat began to leak.
Where were the oars? Left behind at the landing!

readings.title: Rescued by Gilbert (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xxviii, part 2 of 2)
readings.challenge: Track a character’s mixed feelings, including the ones she will not admit.
readings.focus: Anne is saved by the one person she will not forgive, and decides to cure herself of romance.
readings.context: Recap: Playing Tennyson’s Elaine, Anne lay in Mr. Barry’s flat under a black shawl and drifted down the pond toward her friends; but the boat began to leak, the oars were back at the landing, and she saw just one chance of escape. Piles are posts driven into a riverbed to hold up a bridge; drabbled means soaked and muddy; a skiff is a small boat; hysterics is a fit of uncontrolled crying. The amethyst brooch, the Haunted Wood, the liniment cake and the green hair dye are Anne’s earlier scrapes.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXVIII, from Anne’s account of her prayer on the bridge pile to the end of the chapter; opens ““I was horribly frightened,” she told Mrs. Allan the next day, “and it seemed like years…”; closes “…a good thing—not too much, of course—but keep a little of it, Anne, keep a little of it.””.

questions.prompt: Anne tells Mrs. Allan that “it was proper to pray, but I had to do my part.” What does she mean, and what does her prayer show about her?
facilitatorNotes: She prays with her eyes open, watching for a pile, and asks God only to bring the boat close: “I’ll do the rest.” Trust and effort together; she keeps her head when most people would panic. Readers may compare this with her earlier flowery prayers.
evidence: I prayed, Mrs. Allan, most earnestly, but I didn’t shut my eyes to pray
Dear God, please take the flat close to a pile and I’ll do the rest

questions.prompt: Why does Anne refuse Gilbert’s friendship? Find the moment when she nearly accepts.
facilitatorNotes: His half-shy, half-eager look makes her heart give “a quick, queer little beat,” but the memory of “Carrots” and her disgrace stiffens her again, and she refuses coldly. Afterwards she feels “an odd feeling of regret.” The narrator hints that older people would find the grudge laughable; readers can judge whether two years is long enough to forgive.
evidence: Her heart gave a quick, queer little beat.
I shall never be friends with you, Gilbert Blythe; and I don’t want to be!

questions.prompt: Compare the girls’ attempt at rescue with Anne’s own behaviour in danger. What makes their part of the story funny?
facilitatorNotes: Anne kept her self-possession; the others see the flat sink, run off shrieking without once looking toward the bridge, find nobody at home, and leave Ruby in hysterics. The rescue party runs away from the person to be rescued. Jane then calls Gilbert’s rescue romantic, and Anne bans the word.
evidence: never pausing as they crossed the main road to glance the way of the bridge
And I don’t want ever to hear the word romantic again, Jane Andrews.

questions.prompt: Anne lists her mistakes and the fault each one cured. Can she cure herself of romance? What does Matthew advise?
facilitatorNotes: Brooch, meddling; Haunted Wood, imagination run wild; liniment cake, carelessness; dye, vanity; and now romance. Marilla is skeptical. Matthew, alone with her, whispers that a little romance is a good thing. Readers can weigh Anne’s cure against Matthew’s advice, and notice whom the narrator seems to agree with.
evidence: And to-day’s mistake is going to cure me of being too romantic.
Don’t give up all your romance, Anne,” he whispered shyly, “a little of it is a good thing

readings.title: An invitation to town (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xxix, part 1 of 2)
readings.challenge: Notice how description sets a mood, and how Anne’s talk runs ahead of her resolutions.
readings.focus: Diana brings news of a trip to the city, and Anne tries hard not to hope too much.
readings.context: In L. M. Montgomery’s Anne of Green Gables (1908), the orphan Anne Shirley lives with Marilla and Matthew Cuthbert at Green Gables in Avonlea, Prince Edward Island. Diana Barry is her bosom friend. Diana’s great-aunt, Miss Josephine Barry, lives in a grand house in Charlottetown, the island’s capital, and has liked Anne since the night Anne talked her out of a rage. An Exhibition is a large fair with prizes for animals, produce and handiwork. “Marmion” is a long poem by Walter Scott; a canto is one of its parts. A buggy is a light carriage; broadcloth is fine wool cloth; Lovers’ Lane is Anne’s name for a path through the woods.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIX, “An Epoch in Anne’s Life,” from Anne bringing the cows home to the girls in Miss Barry’s parlour; opens “Anne was bringing the cows home from the back pasture by way of Lovers’ Lane. It was a…”; closes “…one consolation when you are poor—there are so many more things you can imagine about.””.

questions.prompt: Read the first paragraph again. Which words make the September evening feel like a painting or a dream?
facilitatorNotes: “Ruby sunset light,” a “clear violet dusk like airy wine,” the wind “out in their tops,” and the narrator’s own claim about the sweetest music on earth. Anne calls it “a purple dream,” echoing the narrator. Readers can choose the phrase that works best for them and say why.
evidence: the spaces under the firs were filled with a clear violet dusk like airy wine
Isn’t this evening just like a purple dream, Diana?

questions.prompt: Why won’t Anne guess eagerly, and why does she refuse to think about the trip until Marilla decides?
facilitatorNotes: She will not “betray too eager curiosity,” for dignity, and she protects herself from disappointment, remembering the hotel concert Marilla refused. Then she talks at length about her new coat and cap. The comedy is the gap between her resolution and her chatter.
evidence: But betray too eager curiosity she would not.
If I did and then was disappointed, it would be more than I could bear.

questions.prompt: Anne asks whether it is wrong to think so much about clothes. What does she believe, and what has changed at Green Gables since Matthew’s Christmas dress?
facilitatorNotes: She says it is “ever so much easier to be good” in fashionable clothes, at least for her. Marilla now makes her dresses fashionably so that Matthew will not go to Mrs. Lynde again, and Matthew has bought her a velvet cap. Readers can judge her claim about clothes and goodness.
evidence: It is ever so much easier to be good if your clothes are fashionable.
Marilla always makes my dresses fashionably now, because she says she doesn’t intend to have Matthew going to Mrs. Lynde to make them.

questions.prompt: In Miss Barry’s parlour, Anne says the splendid room leaves “no scope for imagination.” What does she mean, and do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: Everything is already there and grand, so there is nothing left to imagine; poverty, she says, leaves more room. Diana only wishes a proud schoolmate could see it. Readers may agree, or argue that Anne is consoling herself.
evidence: There are so many things in this room and all so splendid that there is no scope for imagination.
That is one consolation when you are poor—there are so many more things you can imagine about.

readings.title: The best of it all (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xxix, part 2 of 2)
readings.challenge: Listen for what a talkative narrator reveals about herself while describing other things.
readings.focus: Anne enjoys the city and finds out that she belongs at home.
readings.context: Recap: Miss Josephine Barry invited Anne and Diana to stay with her in Charlottetown for the Exhibition. Marilla let Anne go, and after a long early drive the girls were left, a little overawed, in Miss Barry’s grand parlour. A grand stand is the seating for watching races; a prima donna is a leading opera singer; the Academy of Music was a concert hall; Gravenstein is a kind of apple. “Dissipated” here means out late for pleasure. An epoch is a turning point that begins a new period.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIX, from the girls’ days in town to the end of the chapter; opens “Their sojourn in town was something that Anne and Diana dated from for years. From first…”; closes “…I feel that it marks an epoch in my life. But the best of it all was the coming home.””.

questions.prompt: Anne was glad that Josie Pye won a prize, and “glad that I felt glad.” What does that show? Find another moment where she judges her own behaviour.
facilitatorNotes: She watches herself improving: she can now rejoice in a rival’s success. She also refused to bet because she could not tell Mrs. Allan about it, and when the red horse won she concluded that “virtue was its own reward,” having saved ten cents. Readers may find her self-praise funny as well as sincere.
evidence: And I was glad that I felt glad, for it shows I’m improving, don’t you think, Marilla, when I can rejoice in Josie’s success?
So you see that virtue was its own reward.

questions.prompt: How does Anne decide that she “wasn’t born for city life,” and how does Diana differ?
facilitatorNotes: She thinks it over in bed and decides that ice-cream at eleven is lovely once in a while, but she would rather be asleep in the east gable, knowing the stars are shining and the wind is in the firs. Diana believes she was born for city life. Two friends, two tastes; neither is wrong.
evidence: And I came to the conclusion, Marilla, that I wasn’t born for city life and that I was glad of it.
